Title: CBP and DOJ Are Coming For Tariff Errors: How to Protect Your Business
SEO Title: CBP Trade Fraud Enforcement 2026: What Importers Must Know
Story:
CBP and DOJ Are Coming After Tariff Errors. Here Is How to Protect Your Business.

US Customs and Border Protection and the Department of Justice are enforcing trade compliance more aggressively than at any point in recent history. If your import data has gaps, your classifications are inconsistent, or your documentation cannot survive a formal audit, 2026 is the year those problems become expensive.

This is not speculation. The numbers and the enforcement actions tell a clear story that every US importer needs to understand.

The Trade Fraud Task Force Is Real and Active

In August 2025, DOJ launched the Trade Fraud Task Force in partnership with CBP and Homeland Security Investigations. The task force is staffed with 40 attorneys and is designed to coordinate civil and criminal enforcement against importers who evade tariffs, misclassify goods, misrepresent country of origin, or smuggle prohibited products.

Within months of its launch, the task force announced three enforcement actions in a single day, December 18, 2025, recovering over $100 million from companies accused of customs duty evasion. Those cases involved misrepresenting country of origin to avoid Section 301 duties, transshipping Chinese goods through third countries, and knowingly misclassifying products to reduce duty rates.

This is not a task force in name only. It is producing results, and it is scaling up in 2026.

False Claims Act Recoveries Hit a Record

Total recoveries under the False Claims Act reached $6.8 billion in fiscal year 2025, the highest single-year total in the statute's history. A record number of those cases involved customs fraud.

The False Claims Act allows the government to pursue civil penalties against anyone who makes a false statement material to a payment or obligation to the government. In the trade context, that means filing inaccurate entry summaries, underreporting duties owed, or misrepresenting classification, valuation, or country of origin on customs declarations.

Penalties under the FCA can include treble damages, meaning three times the amount of unpaid duties, plus per-claim penalties. For importers with high volumes and systematic errors, the exposure adds up fast.

Equally important: whistleblowers are a primary driver of these cases. Under the FCA's qui tam provisions, employees, competitors, or anyone with knowledge of customs fraud can file a case on behalf of the government and receive up to 30% of any recovery. DOJ has explicitly encouraged customs and trade fraud whistleblowing as a priority area under its Corporate Whistleblower Awards Pilot Program.

CBP Has Better Data Than Ever

CBP is no longer relying solely on random audits and manual reviews. The agency signed a contract with Exiger, giving it access to advanced data analytics tools to cross-reference import data and identify anomalies in classification, valuation, country of origin declarations, and supply chain routing.

This means CBP can now detect patterns that were previously invisible: the same product classified under different HTS codes by different brokers, valuation shifts that do not align with market conditions, origin declarations that are inconsistent with known supply chain logistics, and importers claiming multiple tariff exemptions on the same goods.

The head of the Trade Fraud Task Force, Cody Matthew Herche, confirmed at a February 2026 enforcement forum that investigators are using historical data and case examinations to look for "data shifts that are inconsistent with logistics and that may suggest false statements." He also announced that the task force is engaging with Offices of Inspectors General to identify federal contractors purchasing goods from non-compliant importers.

The IEEPA Refund Process Is Creating Additional Scrutiny

As CBP processes IEEPA tariff refunds, it is simultaneously reviewing the underlying entry data. Importers seeking refunds are seeing an increase in Requests for Information (CF-28s) and Notices of Action (CF-29s) from CBP.

A CF-28 is a request for additional documentation to support how your goods were classified, valued, or declared. A CF-29 is a notice that CBP has already made a change to your entry, often resulting in additional duties owed. Both are signals that CBP is looking more closely at your import history.

For importers with inconsistent data across entries, this is a double-edged situation: you may be entitled to IEEPA refunds on some entries while simultaneously owing additional duties on others where classification or valuation errors are uncovered during the review.

If you are pursuing IEEPA refunds, make sure your underlying entry data is clean before CBP digs into it. Our IEEPA tariff refund guide walks through the full process.

What CBP and DOJ Are Targeting

Based on recent enforcement actions and public statements from task force leadership, here are the specific areas drawing the most scrutiny in 2026.

Country of origin misrepresentation. The largest settlements have involved companies declaring goods as originating from one country when they were actually manufactured in China and transshipped through a third country to avoid Section 301 duties. CBP is using supply chain data to trace actual manufacturing locations and compare them against declared origins.

HTS misclassification. Both intentional and negligent misclassification are being pursued. Intentional misclassification to reduce duties is treated as fraud. But even negligent misclassification, where a company simply did not exercise "reasonable care" in determining the correct code, can result in penalties under Section 1592 of the Tariff Act of 1930, with penalties up to the domestic value of the merchandise.

Valuation manipulation. Double-invoicing schemes, where an importer submits a lower-value invoice to CBP while billing customers at the actual price, are a specific enforcement target. CBP is also scrutinizing valuation methodologies that lack supporting documentation.

Transshipment and tariff evasion. Routing goods through third countries to avoid country-specific duties is being tracked using data analytics. This includes Section 301, Section 232, and antidumping/countervailing duty evasion.

Drawback abuse. Overstating or misrepresenting export volumes to inflate duty drawback claims is being monitored more closely as duty drawback programs grow.

What This Means for Manufacturers and Importers

If you are an import-heavy manufacturer, the enforcement environment demands a specific set of actions. These are not optional compliance best practices. They are risk mitigation steps that directly affect your financial exposure.

Standardize your HTS classifications across all brokers. One of the most common problems we see at GingerControl is different customs brokers classifying the same part under different HTS codes. This creates systematic duty inconsistencies that are exactly the kind of data anomaly CBP's analytics tools are designed to flag. A single, defensible classification for each product, documented with clear reasoning and references, eliminates this risk.

Audit your country of origin determinations. If your supply chain involves components manufactured in one country and assembled or finished in another, make sure your origin determinations follow the substantial transformation test and are backed by documentation. If you source from countries subject to Section 301 tariffs, your origin claims will receive extra scrutiny.

Document your valuation methodology. CBP expects importers to have a clear, consistent, and documented approach to how they determine the declared value of imported goods. If your methodology is ad hoc or undocumented, you are vulnerable.

Review your duty drawback claims. If you participate in a duty drawback program, make sure your export documentation, HTS matching, and claim calculations are accurate and traceable. Drawback abuse is a named enforcement priority.

Consider voluntary self-disclosure. If you discover compliance problems during an internal review, DOJ has made clear that voluntary self-disclosure, cooperation, and remediation lead to substantially more favorable outcomes. Companies that come forward before being investigated receive significant settlement credit under both DOJ's Corporate Enforcement Policy and the FCA.

Treat compliance as a financial function, not just a legal one. The companies that get caught are typically the ones where compliance sits in a silo, disconnected from finance, procurement, and operations. When trade compliance is integrated into your financial planning, classification errors get caught earlier, duty savings get captured, and audit exposure shrinks.

Get Ahead of Enforcement

The cost of getting caught is measured in multiples of what it costs to get compliant. A single misclassification error replicated across thousands of entries can produce seven-figure penalties. A country of origin misrepresentation can result in criminal prosecution of individual employees.

Title: Section 122 Tariffs: What US Importers Need to Know Before July 24
SEO Title: Section 122 Tariffs Explained: What Expires July 24, 2026
Story:
Section 122 Tariffs Explained: What US Importers Need to Know Before July 24

On February 24, 2026, a new 15% global tariff took effect on most goods entering the United States. It was imposed under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, a statute that had never been used at this scale before. And it expires on July 24, 2026.

If you import goods into the US, this tariff is already affecting your landed costs. But because it is temporary by law, the real question is what happens next. This guide explains what Section 122 is, how it works, what is exempt, and what importers should be doing right now to prepare for what comes after.

What Is Section 122 and Why Does It Exist?

Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 gives the president authority to impose temporary import surcharges to address "fundamental international payments problems," specifically large balance-of-payments deficits. It was designed as an emergency economic tool, not a long-term trade policy instrument.

The administration invoked Section 122 on February 20, 2026, hours after the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump. The IEEPA tariffs had been the backbone of the administration's trade policy since early 2025, with country-specific rates reaching as high as 145% on Chinese goods. When the Supreme Court ruled that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, the administration needed a replacement immediately.

Section 122 was that replacement. The initial rate was set at 10%, then raised to 15% (the statutory maximum) two days later. It took effect at 12:01 a.m. on February 24, the exact moment CBP stopped collecting IEEPA duties.

The administration has been clear that Section 122 is a stopgap. The real long-term tariff strategy will come through expanded use of Section 232 (national security) and Section 301 (unfair trade practices), both of which require formal investigations and public comment periods before tariffs can be imposed.

How Section 122 Differs from the IEEPA Tariffs It Replaced

Understanding what changed between the IEEPA regime and Section 122 is critical for importers recalculating their landed costs.

Rate structure. IEEPA tariffs were country-specific. Different trading partners faced different rates based on bilateral negotiations. Under Section 122, the rate is a flat 15% applied uniformly to all countries. There are no country-specific adjustments.

Rate cap. Section 122 has a statutory ceiling of 15%. IEEPA had no cap, which is how rates on Chinese imports reached 145%. For many importers sourcing from high-tariff countries under IEEPA, the shift to Section 122 actually reduced their duty burden. For importers sourcing from countries that had negotiated low IEEPA rates, the opposite may be true.

Time limit. Section 122 tariffs can only last 150 days unless Congress votes to extend them. The current tariff expires on July 24, 2026. IEEPA tariffs had no expiration date.

Uniformity requirement. Section 122 requires "broad and uniform application." The tariff must apply globally. This means the administration cannot use Section 122 to impose higher rates on specific countries the way it did with IEEPA.

Stacking rules. Section 122 tariffs do not stack on top of Section 232 tariffs. If your product is already subject to a 232 duty (steel at 50%, aluminum at 50%, autos at 25%, etc.), the Section 122 surcharge does not apply to that product. However, Section 122 does stack on top of Section 301 tariffs and normal MFN duty rates.

Trade-weighted average. According to analysis from Global Trade Alert, the trade-weighted average US tariff rate under Section 122 at 15% is approximately 13.0%, compared to 15.2% before the Supreme Court ruling and 8.1% if no replacement tariff had been enacted.

What Is Exempt from Section 122 Tariffs?

The proclamation includes two annexes that define which products are excluded from the 15% surcharge. Approximately 1,100 product codes are listed in Annex II as fully exempt.

Products already covered by Section 232 tariffs are the largest exemption category. This includes steel and aluminum (50%), copper and derivatives (50%), automobiles and auto parts (25%), semiconductors (25%), and lumber and timber (10%). Because Section 122 does not stack on top of 232, these products continue to pay their existing 232 rates with no additional surcharge.

USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt if they meet the rules of origin requirements under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement. This is significant for manufacturers with North American supply chains.

CAFTA-DR qualifying goods, including textile and apparel articles from Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Nicaragua, are also exempt.

Other product exemptions in Annex II cover certain agricultural products (including beef, tomatoes, and oranges), critical minerals, pharmaceuticals and pharmaceutical ingredients, energy and energy products, certain electronics, and civil aircraft and parts covered under the 1979 Agreement on Trade in Civil Aircraft.

Humanitarian goods such as food, clothing, and medicine donated for relief purposes are exempt.

Important note on classification: These exemptions are triggered by HTS code, not by product description. If your product is misclassified, the exemption does not apply even if the product description seems to match. This is one of the most common and costly errors importers make. Accurate HTS classification is the foundation of determining whether you owe the 15% surcharge or not.

What Happens on July 24, 2026?

This is the question every importer should be planning around. Section 122 tariffs expire after 150 days by statute. The administration cannot extend them unilaterally. Only Congress can vote to keep them in place past July 24.

The administration has already signaled its plan for what comes next. There are three main pathways:

New Section 301 investigations. USTR announced the initiation of new Section 301 investigations into unfair trade practices by US trading partners. The specific countries have not been named yet. Section 301 allows country-specific tariffs after a formal investigation, public comment period, and findings of unfair practices. This process takes months, but the administration appears to be moving quickly.

Expanded Section 232 tariffs. Multiple Section 232 investigations are pending on pharmaceuticals, commercial aircraft, wind turbines, robotics, drones, and medical devices. Any of these could produce new tariffs before or shortly after July 24. The administration has been accelerating these investigations well beyond the normal 270-day timeline.

Congressional action. If Congress passes legislation, Section 122 tariffs could be extended or replaced with a permanent tariff structure. Given the current political environment, this remains uncertain.

For importers, the practical implication is that the tariff landscape will almost certainly change again on or around July 24. The replacement may be higher, lower, or differently structured depending on which statutory authorities the administration uses and how quickly investigations are completed.

What Importers Should Do Right Now

The Section 122 tariff is already in effect and already affecting your costs. Here is how to respond.

Verify your exemption eligibility. Review every product you import against the Annex II exemption list. Remember: exemptions are based on HTS classification, not product description. If you are not confident in your codes, get them reviewed. A misclassified product could mean paying 15% unnecessarily, or claiming an exemption you are not entitled to (which creates audit risk).

Recalculate your landed costs. If you previously sourced from countries with high IEEPA rates (India, Thailand, Vietnam, for example), your duty burden may have decreased under Section 122. If you sourced from countries with low negotiated IEEPA rates, it may have increased. Update your cost models.

Review your Section 232 exposure. Products covered by Section 232 are exempt from Section 122. But the definition of what counts as a Section 232 product, especially for derivative articles containing steel, aluminum, or copper, can be complex. Make sure you are classifying the metal and non-metal content of mixed products correctly, as the Section 122 surcharge may still apply to the non-metal portion.

Understand the stacking. Section 122 stacks on top of Section 301 tariffs and normal MFN rates, but not on top of Section 232. If you import Chinese-origin goods, your total stack is MFN rate + Section 301 rate + 15% Section 122. That can add up fast.

Plan for July 24. Start modeling scenarios for what happens when Section 122 expires. Will your products be subject to new Section 301 tariffs? New Section 232 tariffs? Nothing? The importers who run these scenarios now will be better positioned to adjust pricing, sourcing, and inventory strategies before the transition.

Monitor regulatory updates. Subscribe to CBP's Cargo Systems Messaging Service (CSMS) for operational guidance. Watch for USTR Federal Register notices on Section 301 investigation timelines. Follow Section 232 investigation developments through the Department of Commerce.

Check Your Classifications

Whether you are paying the Section 122 surcharge, claiming an Annex II exemption, or navigating the overlap with Section 232, everything starts with having the right HTS codes. A single misclassification can mean overpaying duties, losing an exemption, or triggering a CBP audit.

Title: How to Claim Your IEEPA Tariff Refund: A Guide for US Importers
SEO Title: IEEPA Tariff Refund: Step-by-Step Guide for US Importers
Story:
How to Claim Your IEEPA Tariff Refund: A Step-by-Step Guide for US Importers

If you paid IEEPA tariffs on imports between February 2025 and February 2026, you are likely owed a refund. The Supreme Court ruled those tariffs unlawful, and the Court of International Trade has ordered CBP to begin processing refunds for all importers of record, not just those who filed lawsuits.

The money is real. Estimates place total IEEPA refunds at roughly $175 billion across all affected importers. But the process is still taking shape, and importers who prepare now will be first in line when CBP opens the floodgates.

This guide walks you through exactly how to determine your eligibility, calculate what you are owed, and take the right steps to claim your IEEPA tariff refund.

Who Is Eligible for an IEEPA Tariff Refund?

You are eligible if you were the importer of record on any US customs entries that included IEEPA duties. This covers two main categories of tariffs:

Fentanyl tariffs, imposed on imports from Canada, Mexico, and China starting February 4, 2025. These were designed to address drug trafficking and immigration concerns.

Reciprocal tariffs, imposed on imports from most other US trading partners starting April 2, 2025. These were the broad, country-specific tariffs that reached as high as 145% on Chinese goods.

Both categories were struck down by the Supreme Court on February 20, 2026. IEEPA tariffs on imports from Venezuela, Brazil, and Russia are also covered.

If you are not the importer of record (for example, if your freight forwarder or a third-party logistics provider served as the nominal IOR), your path to a refund is more complicated. You may need their cooperation to file claims, or you may have contractual rights to recover tariff costs that were passed through to you. Review your supplier and broker agreements now.

How to Calculate What You Are Owed

Before you can claim a refund, you need to know exactly how much you paid in IEEPA duties. Here is how to find that number.

Step 1: Log into your ACE portal.

The Automated Commercial Environment is CBP's system for all import and export data. If you do not have an ACE account, apply for one immediately at CBP's website. Processing times are currently slower than usual due to the volume of applications, so do not delay.

Step 2: Run the Entry Summary details report (ES-003).

This report can be exported to a spreadsheet. It contains every entry summary line for your imports, including the HTS codes and duty amounts assessed.

Step 3: Filter for IEEPA tariff codes.

Look for HTS codes beginning with 9903.01 (the fentanyl tariffs on Canada, Mexico, and China) and 9903.02 (the reciprocal tariffs). Filter further at the eight-digit level by country to see exactly which entries were subject to IEEPA duties and how much was assessed.

Step 4: Calculate the total with interest.

Add up the IEEPA duty amounts across all affected entries. Interest accrues at rates published quarterly by the IRS in the Federal Register. Each month the government delays repayment, interest continues to accumulate, currently estimated at roughly $700 million per month across all importers.

If your import volume is high or your data is spread across multiple customs brokers, this process can be complex. Getting your HTS classifications right is critical here, because misclassified entries may have been assessed incorrect IEEPA rates or may not show up in the right filter. Check your classifications with our HTS Classification Assistant →

Understanding Liquidation Status: Why It Matters

Your refund path depends on whether your entries are liquidated or unliquidated. This is the single most important distinction in the refund process.

Unliquidated entries are imports where CBP has not yet issued its final duty calculation. CBP has up to 314 days after entry to liquidate. For these entries, the Court of International Trade has ordered CBP to liquidate them without regard to IEEPA duties, meaning the refund should happen automatically as part of the normal liquidation process.

Liquidated entries are imports where CBP has already issued its final duty calculation. If liquidation is not yet final (meaning fewer than 180 days have passed since the liquidation date), the CIT ordered CBP to reliquidate them without IEEPA duties. This should also result in a refund without requiring the importer to take further action, if the CIT's order stands.

Entries where liquidation is final, meaning more than 180 days have passed since liquidation and no protest was filed, are the most uncertain category. The CIT's March 4 order did not explicitly address these entries. Importers with significant duty exposure in this category may want to consult a trade attorney.

The key takeaway: Check the liquidation status of every entry that included IEEPA duties. Your ACE portal shows this information. Entries that are still unliquidated or recently liquidated are in the strongest position for refunds.

What to Do Right Now: A Practical Checklist

The refund process is still evolving. CBP has indicated it is building new ACE functionality to handle IEEPA refund declarations, which it expects to have ready within approximately 45 days (around mid-April 2026). In the meantime, here is what importers should do now.

1. Get your ACE account set up. If you do not already have one, apply immediately. You need this to access your import data, track liquidation status, and eventually file refund claims.

2. Register for ACH refunds. CBP will issue refunds electronically via Automated Clearing House. Make sure your ACH information is on file with CBP. This requires an active ACE account.

3. Preserve all documentation. Gather and securely store entry summaries (CF-7501), commercial invoices, packing slips, bills of lading, and any internal records showing how tariff costs were allocated. You will need these to support your refund claim and to respond to any CBP requests for information.

4. Audit your entry data for accuracy. This is where many importers find problems. If different customs brokers classified the same product under different HTS codes, your IEEPA duty amounts may be inconsistent. Inaccurate classifications can mean you overpaid on some entries and underpaid on others, and CBP is already issuing an increased volume of Requests for Information (CF-28s) and Notices of Action (CF-29s) as it reviews entries during the refund process.

5. Monitor your liquidation deadlines. For liquidated entries, the 180-day protest window is running. Track every entry's liquidation date and calendar the protest deadline. Missing this window could forfeit your refund rights for those entries.

6. Consider filing protective protests. For entries that have already liquidated, filing a protest within the 180-day window preserves your rights even while the broader refund process is being sorted out. This is especially important if the government successfully appeals the CIT's March 4 order.

7. Watch for CBP guidance. CBP is expected to issue further instructions through the Cargo Systems Messaging Service (CSMS) and the Federal Register. Subscribe to CSMS updates and monitor CBP's IEEPA FAQ page for the latest procedural guidance.

What About Downstream Buyers?

If you are not the importer of record but your suppliers passed IEEPA tariff costs through to you in the form of price increases or surcharges, you may have a claim against them when they receive their refund.

This is especially relevant for manufacturers who purchase imported components from distributors or intermediaries. If your supplier documented the tariff pass-through in writing (such as price increase notices, tariff surcharge line items on invoices, or cost-plus contract structures), you have a stronger basis for recovery.

The practical step: send a written preservation-of-rights notice to your key suppliers now, asserting your claim to a share of any IEEPA tariff refund attributable to goods you purchased. Do not wait until the refund is issued. Establish your position early.

What This Does Not Change

The IEEPA refund process only covers tariffs imposed under IEEPA. The following tariffs remain fully in effect and are not eligible for refunds:

  • Section 232 tariffs on steel (50%), aluminum (50%), copper (50%), automobiles (25%), semiconductors (25%), lumber (10%), and other covered products

  • Section 301 tariffs on Chinese-origin goods (7.5% to 100%)

  • Section 122 tariffs, the 15% global tariff imposed on February 24, 2026, which expires July 24, 2026

  • Antidumping and countervailing duties on specific products and countries

If your total duty burden still feels high after IEEPA refunds, it may be worth reviewing your broader tariff strategy. Misclassifications, missed duty drawback opportunities, or suboptimal country of origin determinations could be costing you more than you realize.

Get a Clear Picture of What You Are Owed

Navigating the IEEPA refund process starts with accurate data: the right HTS codes, the right entry records, and a clear understanding of your exposure.

Title: Trade Compliance in March 2026: What US Importers Need to Know
SEO Title: Trade Compliance March 2026: Tariff Updates for US Importers
Story:
Trade Compliance in March 2026: What US Importers Need to Know

March 2026 may be the most consequential month for US trade compliance in a generation. The Supreme Court struck down IEEPA tariffs, a replacement tariff took effect overnight, and CBP is ramping up enforcement across the board. If you import goods into the United States, especially as a manufacturer, here is what changed, what it means, and what you should do about it.

This is your trade compliance March 2026 briefing.

The IEEPA Tariff Ruling and What It Means for Refunds

On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize the president to impose tariffs. The decision invalidated both the "reciprocal" tariffs on most US trading partners and the fentanyl-related tariffs on China, Canada, and Mexico that had been in place since early 2025.

The ruling itself was clear: IEEPA is not a tariff statute. But the refund process has been anything but simple.

On March 4, the Court of International Trade ordered CBP to begin processing refunds for all importers not just those who filed lawsuits. Judge Richard Eaton wrote that all importers of record whose entries were subject to IEEPA duties are entitled to the benefit of the Supreme Court's decision. The government is expected to appeal.

What importers should know right now:

  • All IEEPA tariffs paid since February 2025 (fentanyl tariffs) and April 2025 (reciprocal tariffs) through February 24, 2026 are potentially eligible for refunds

  • Estimates place total refunds owed at roughly $175 billion across all importers

  • CBP stopped assessing IEEPA duties on entries made after February 24, 2026

  • The refund timeline remains uncertain, CBP's systems were not designed for mass refunds at this scale

  • Importers should preserve all entry summaries, duty payment documentation, and internal records of tariff costs immediately

If you paid IEEPA duties over the past year, you likely have money coming back. The question is when and how. We covered the initial ruling in detail in our IEEPA Supreme Court ruling compliance roadmap.

Section 122: The Replacement Tariff

Hours after the Supreme Court's decision, President Trump issued a proclamation imposing a 10% global tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974. This took effect on February 24, 2026. The rate was later raised to 15%.

Section 122 is a fundamentally different tool than IEEPA. Here is how they compare:

  • Rate cap: Section 122 tariffs are capped at 15%. IEEPA tariffs had no cap, rates on Chinese imports reached as high as 145%.

  • Time limit: Section 122 tariffs expire after 150 days (July 24, 2026) unless Congress votes to extend them.

  • Scope: Section 122 tariffs must apply globally and uniformly. They cannot be country-specific the way IEEPA tariffs were.

  • Stacking: Section 122 tariffs do not stack on top of Section 232 tariffs. Products already subject to 232 duties (steel, aluminum, autos) are exempt from the additional 122 surcharge.

Key exemptions from the Section 122 tariff include:

  • Goods already subject to Section 232 tariffs (steel, aluminum, copper, autos, semiconductors)

  • Certain agricultural products, pharmaceuticals, energy products, and critical minerals

  • Civil aircraft and parts covered under the 1979 Agreement on Trade in Civil Aircraft

  • Canadian and Mexican goods that qualify under USMCA

The administration has signaled that Section 122 is a stopgap. Expect new Section 301 and Section 232 investigations to produce longer-term tariff structures before the July 24 expiration.

Section 301 China Tariffs: Still in Effect, Still Stacking

While the IEEPA tariffs are gone, Section 301 tariffs on Chinese-origin goods remain fully in place. These range from 7.5% to 100% depending on the product and the specific tariff list.

These duties stack on top of normal trade relations (NTR/MFN) duty rates and any applicable Section 232 duties. For many importers sourcing from China, the total duty burden has not meaningfully decreased, it has simply shifted legal footing.

USTR has also announced new Section 301 investigations into unfair trade practices. Countries targeted by these investigations have not yet been named, but the administration has made clear that Section 301 will be a primary tool going forward.

For manufacturers importing Chinese-origin components or raw materials, this is not the time to assume tariff relief is coming. Review your HTS classification strategy and make sure your codes are accurate and defensible.

Section 232 Tariffs Are Expanding

Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act allows tariffs on imports that threaten national security. The current administration has used this authority aggressively. Since January 2025, 12 new Section 232 investigations have been initiated, more than in any previous administration.

Currently in effect:

  • Steel and aluminum: 50%

  • Copper and derivatives: 50%

  • Automobiles and auto parts: 25%

  • Semiconductors (certain AI chips): 25%

  • Lumber and timber: 10%

  • Upholstered furniture: 30% (increasing from 25% as of January 2026)

  • Kitchen cabinets and vanities: 50%

Investigations still pending that could produce new tariffs:

  • Pharmaceuticals

  • Commercial aircraft and jet engines

  • Wind turbines

  • Robotics and industrial machinery

  • Unmanned aircraft systems (drones)

  • Personal protective equipment and medical devices

  • Polysilicon and derivatives

For import-heavy manufacturers, the Section 232 landscape demands proactive classification review. A product that was not subject to 232 duties six months ago may be subject to them by summer. If your supply chain touches any of these categories, start preparing now.

De Minimis Is Gone

The Section 321 de minimis exemption, which allowed shipments valued under $800 to enter the US duty-free, was suspended in August 2025 for all countries. This is now the new normal.

Every shipment entering the United States, regardless of value, now requires formal customs entry with full documentation: commercial invoices, packing lists, 10-digit HTS classification, and valuation. Duties, taxes, and brokerage fees apply across the board.

For e-commerce businesses, this was a dramatic shift. But manufacturers importing low-value components, samples, or spare parts are also affected. If your supply chain includes any small-value shipments that previously cleared under Section 321, those now require the same customs treatment as any other import.

Congress has also passed legislation making the de minimis elimination permanent effective July 1, 2027, removing any possibility of the exemption being reinstated.

CBP Enforcement Is Escalating

US Customs and Border Protection is investing heavily in enforcement. The agency launched a Trade Fraud Task Force staffed with 40 attorneys focused on tariff evasion, transshipment, false valuation, misclassification, and fraudulent origin claims.

CBP also signed a contract with Exiger, giving the agency access to expanded data analytics for targeting suspicious entries. This means CBP can now cross-reference import data more effectively to identify inconsistencies in classification, valuation, and country of origin declarations.

For importers, the message is clear: documentation standards matter more than ever. If your HTS classifications are inconsistent across brokers, your valuation methodology is undocumented, or your country of origin determinations are not backed by supporting records, you are at elevated risk.

This is especially relevant for manufacturers using multiple customs brokers. We have seen firsthand how different brokers classify the same part under different HTS codes, creating systematic duty overpayments and audit exposure. Standardizing your classification is one of the highest-ROI compliance actions you can take right now.

What Importers Should Do Right Now

March 2026 is not the month to wait and see. Here is a practical checklist:

  1. Preserve your IEEPA records. Gather all entry summaries, duty payments, and internal documentation for entries made between February 2025 and February 2026. You will need these for refund claims.

  2. Audit your HTS classifications. With tariffs shifting across multiple authorities, an incorrect code can mean paying the wrong rate, or triggering penalties. Make sure your classifications are current, consistent, and defensible.

  3. Map your Section 232 exposure. Review whether any of your imported products fall within pending investigation categories (pharma, aircraft, robotics, drones, PPE). If they do, model the cost impact now.

  4. Review your Section 301 position. If you source from China, confirm your total duty burden under the current rate structure. Look for legitimate tariff mitigation opportunities like duty drawback or reclassification.

  5. Strengthen your documentation. CBP is targeting valuation, classification, and origin claims. Ensure every import has a clear, traceable paper trail that can withstand an audit.

  6. Monitor the Section 122 expiration. The current 15% global tariff expires July 24, 2026. Whatever replaces it, whether through Congressional action, new Section 301 investigations, or expanded Section 232 tariffs, will reshape your cost structure again.

Try Our HTS Classification Assistant

Getting your tariff classifications right is the foundation of everything else, refund eligibility, duty optimization, audit readiness, and compliance risk management.

Title: Secondary HTS Codes: What They Are and Why They Matter
SEO Title: Secondary HTS Codes Guide: Chapter 99 Tariff Compliance
Story:
The Structure of an USHTS Code

Before getting into secondary codes, a foundation: the US Harmonized Tariff Schedule operates on a ten-digit structure. The first six digits are the international Harmonized System code identical across nearly all WTO member countries. Digits seven through ten are US-specific, added to support domestic trade policy and statistical reporting needs.

The primary ten-digit code you assign to an imported product determines your base MFN (Most Favored Nation) duty rate the column 1 rate assessed on imports from all WTO members in good standing.

But the US tariff system has additional rate layers applied through overlay duties. Section 301 China tariffs. Section 232 steel and aluminum duties. Antidumping and countervailing duties. IEEPA emergency tariffs. These overlays are assessed through a secondary code system operating inside CBP's Automated Commercial Environment (ACE), and they are where most compliance errors and most overpayments hide.

What Secondary HTS Codes Actually Are

In ACE, importers file entries with a primary HTS code plus additional codes for any applicable duty overlays. These codes drawn from Chapter 99 of the HTSUS — are the mechanism through which CBP assesses duties beyond the base MFN rate.

Chapter 99 is a domestic chapter not part of the international Harmonized System. It exists specifically for temporary and special duty provisions. The 9903.XX.XX codes it contains cover:

Section 301 tariff codes. Chinese-origin goods on USTR Lists 1 through 4 each have corresponding 9903 codes that trigger the applicable surcharge rate — from 7.5% to 25% depending on the list and product.

Section 232 tariff codes. Steel and aluminum imports carry 9903 codes that apply the 25% steel duty or the 25% aluminum duty (as expanded in 2024), with country-specific exclusions handled through separate exclusion codes.

Section 201 safeguard codes. Applied to solar cells, washing machines, and other products that received safeguard protection under Section 201 proceedings.

Antidumping and countervailing duty codes. AD/CVD orders maintain separate chapter 99 entries that trigger the cash deposit or bond requirement for covered products from covered countries.

IEEPA tariff codes. The executive order tariffs imposed beginning in early 2025 were implemented through new 9903 codes in ACE. The Supreme Court's February 20, 2026 ruling invalidating certain IEEPA applications led to rapid deactivation of some of these codes. Importers who were still filing deactivated IEEPA codes after February 23 were filing incorrect entries.

Exclusion codes. Temporary exclusions from Section 301 or Section 232 tariffs for specific products or companies have their own 9903 codes that counteract the applicable surcharge. These codes have expiration dates. Codes that expire do not automatically remove themselves from your entry templates.

Why Secondary HTS Code Errors Are Common

Classification decisions do not automatically follow product changes. When a product's primary HTS code changes — because of a product modification, a supplier change, or a tariff schedule update — the Chapter 99 secondary codes need to be reviewed too. They are linked to the primary code's applicability. If your product moved to a different primary classification, the secondary codes may change as well. Manual classification processes frequently miss this linkage.

Exclusions expire without warning. During the peak of Section 301 tariff implementation, USTR issued thousands of product-specific exclusions. These exclusions were time-limited, typically one to two years, and required renewal petitions before expiration. Companies that received exclusions and embedded the exclusion code into their entry templates sometimes continued using the code after it lapsed — claiming duty exemptions they were no longer entitled to. CBP has found these systematically during post-entry audits and assessed the unpaid duties plus interest.

IEEPA codes changed faster than manual processes could track. The February 2026 IEEPA situation illustrates how quickly the secondary code environment can shift. Executive orders created new IEEPA overlay tariffs overnight. CBP published updated ACE chapter 99 codes on an expedited basis. Importers had days, not weeks, to update entry templates and inform their brokers. Companies relying on manual entry processes or brokers without automated regulatory feeds filed entries with incorrect secondary codes during the transition — either paying tariffs that were suddenly inapplicable or missing new obligations.

Country of origin errors cascade into secondary code errors. Secondary code obligations for Section 301 purposes depend on whether goods are of Chinese origin. If your country of origin determination is wrong — either incorrectly claiming Chinese origin or incorrectly claiming third-country origin — the secondary code selection follows the error. Layer two problems frequently trace to layer one mistakes in origin analysis.

The Secondary Tariff Complication

In 2025, "secondary tariffs" became a distinct policy concept separate from the secondary HTS code mechanism — but confusingly adjacent in terminology.

Secondary tariffs as a policy tool are tariffs applied to countries that continue trading with a sanctioned or targeted country. The US explored this concept for countries maintaining trade relationships with Russia and China under specific conditions. Several trade policy proposals have centered secondary tariff exposure on how a third country's trade relationship with China affects the duty treatment of that country's exports to the US.

For compliance teams, the immediate implication is that country of origin analysis now needs to consider not just the rules of origin for the goods themselves, but the geopolitical context of the countries in your supply chain. A product of Vietnamese origin that contains significant Chinese-origin components may face different treatment depending on US assessments of Vietnam's overall sourcing relationships.

The regulatory framework for secondary tariffs of this type is still developing. But waiting for clarity before mapping your exposure is not a strategy. The companies getting ahead of this are documenting their full supply chain origin picture now — not because the rules are final, but because the documentation infrastructure takes time to build.

Keeping Your Secondary Codes Accurate

Maintain a living classification document. For each active import product, track: primary HTSUS code, applicable Chapter 99 secondary codes and their basis, current duty rates including all overlays, any active exclusions and their expiration dates, and the country of origin determination supporting the secondary code selection. Update this document whenever any element changes — product modification, supplier switch, regulatory update, exclusion expiration.

Set monitoring alerts for 9903 code changes. CBP publishes updates to Chapter 99 when new trade measures take effect or existing ones are modified. The Federal Register, CBP's trade website, and USTR announcements are your primary sources. For companies without automated monitoring, this means checking regularly rather than waiting for a broker to surface the change.

Run a periodic secondary code audit. At least quarterly, pull a sample of recent import entries and compare the secondary codes actually filed against what should have been filed based on current regulations. Discrepancies flag either a process error — your broker used the wrong code — or an update that was not communicated — a code changed and your process did not catch it. Finding these in an internal audit is significantly less expensive than finding them in a CBP audit.

Build update communication protocols with your broker. Secondary code updates happen frequently during active trade policy periods. Your customs broker should have a defined protocol for communicating significant code changes — alerting you to the change and confirming the updated procedure — not just silently implementing them on the next entry. If your broker relationship does not include that communication layer, that is a gap worth closing.

Scope your IEEPA period exposure now. If you had entries filed during the period when IEEPA codes were active — roughly mid-2025 through February 23, 2026 — and those entries are still unliquidated, you may have duty refund eligibility under the Supreme Court ruling. The protest window runs from the date of liquidation. Identifying that exposure now, before entries liquidate and the protest window closes, is the time-sensitive piece.

How AI Handles Secondary Code Complexity

Manual secondary code management works reasonably well when trade policy is stable and the overlay system is static. It breaks down under the volume and frequency of updates that have characterized the 2023 to 2026 period.

AI classification systems that stay current with regulatory feeds can maintain the Chapter 99 code layer automatically, applying the correct overlay codes based on current regulations, current product classification, and current origin determination. When IEEPA codes change, the system updates. When exclusions expire, the system removes them. When new Section 301 determinations are published, the system applies the corresponding 9903 codes.

The value is not just accuracy on any single entry. It is speed across all entries. In February 2026, when IEEPA codes were being deactivated and CBP was updating ACE on a compressed timeline, companies with AI-fed classification systems adapted almost immediately. Companies with manual processes spent those same days manually updating templates across hundreds of SKUs and communicating with brokers who were simultaneously managing the same transition for dozens of clients.

OpenClaw tracks active Chapter 99 codes in real time. If you want to confirm that your current secondary code assignments reflect today's regulations — not last quarter's — the simulator will show you the complete tariff picture for your product and origin combination.

The Classification Program That Covers Both Layers

The importers who navigated 2025 and into 2026 without CBP penalty notices are not the ones with the most resources. They are the ones with the cleanest, most current classification data.

That means primary codes that are accurate and defensible. It means secondary codes that reflect current overlay requirements, including any recent changes. It means country of origin documentation that supports both the primary classification and the secondary code selection. And it means a monitoring process that catches regulatory updates before they affect the next shipment.

Getting secondary HTS codes wrong creates the same liability as getting primary codes wrong, unpaid duties, interest, penalties, and the audit risk that follows. The fix is the same: build the classification program that covers both layers and keeps them current.

Secondary HTS codes are Chapter 99 overlay codes filed in CBP's ACE system alongside your primary 10-digit HTS code. They trigger additional duties beyond the base MFN rate, including Section 301 China tariffs, Section 232 steel and aluminum duties, antidumping deposits, and IEEPA surcharges.

Title: What the Supreme Court's IEEPA Ruling Means for Importers
SEO Title: IEEPA Supreme Court Ruling: Importer Compliance Guide
Story:
The U.S. Supreme Court just struck down the legal basis for every tariff imposed under IEEPA since February 2025.

This morning, six justices ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act is an emergency sanctions law. Not a general trade law. It can't be used to raise revenue through tariffs.

Translation: All existing IEEPA-based tariffs are legally vulnerable. Right now.

Trump announced within hours that he'll use alternative legal authorities (Section 301, Section 232, reciprocal tariffs under different statutes). But which ones will survive legal challenge? That's now an open question.

Your compliance team needs to understand what just happened, what's at risk, and what to do in the next 90 days while the administration figures out its next move.

What the Ruling Actually Says

The Supreme Court was asked a simple question: Can the President use IEEPA to impose tariffs as a trade policy tool?

The answer: No.

Here's why. IEEPA is Title II of the National Emergencies Act. It was designed for sanctions. For blocking enemy assets. For freezing transactions with adversaries. It explicitly authorizes the President to "regulate, or prohibit, any transactions in foreign exchange...and the transfer of credit, payments and remittances."

That's about controlling money flows, not setting duty rates.

Congress gave the President other tools for trade policy. Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act. Reciprocal tariff authority under other statutes.

But IEEPA? That's not a trade tool. It's a sanctions tool.

The Court said using it for tariffs is like using a fire hose to water your garden. Technically it's water, but you're using the wrong tool for the job.

What This Means for Duties You Already Paid

Here's where it gets real.

Between February 2025 and today, importers paid duties under IEEPA-based tariffs. Billions of dollars in duties. Those duties were collected under an authority the Supreme Court just said the President didn't have.

That opens the door to refund claims.

This is not speculation. Law firms are already filing suits. Customs brokers are advising clients to file refund protests. The CBP Commissioner's office is preparing for a surge of refund requests.

If you imported goods subject to IEEPA tariffs and paid duties, you now have a legal claim that those duties were illegally collected.

Three questions your compliance team should answer RIGHT NOW:

  1. What duties did we pay under IEEPA authority between Feb 2025 and today?

    • Pull entry records for all shipments subject to tariffs announced under IEEPA

    • Quantify total duties paid

    • This is your refund baseline

  2. Do we have the documentation to support a refund claim?

    • Invoice copies

    • Entry records

    • Proof of payment

    • Companies with clean records win refunds faster

  3. Which refund path makes sense for our situation?

    • Direct refund request to CBP (faster, for smaller claims)

    • Refund protest (formal, for contested amounts)

    • Class-action lawsuit (if your duties are substantial and CBP drags feet)

    • Work with customs broker or trade counsel

What Happens in the Next 90 Days

The administration won't leave importers in limbo for long. Trump signaled a new 10% global tariff via "alternative legal avenues" within hours of the ruling.

But which authorities will they use?

Section 301 (Trade Retaliation)

  • Strongest legal ground

  • Historically survived court challenges

  • Applies to specific countries (likely China)

  • Risk: Still precedent for legal challenges

Section 232 (National Security)

  • Used for steel/aluminum tariffs

  • Courts generally defer to President on national security

  • But scope is narrower (specific products, countries)

  • Risk: Courts have questioned whether some products qualify

Reciprocal Tariff Authority

  • Trump's preferred approach

  • Legal basis less established

  • Congress never explicitly delegated this authority

  • Risk: Highest risk of legal challenge

Other Trade Statutes

  • Safeguard tariffs (temporary, narrow)

  • Countervailing duties (anti-dumping)

  • These are narrower and don't solve Trump's global tariff ambition

The point: The administration has options, but each one has legal vulnerabilities. None will be as fast or as sweeping as IEEPA was.

What this means for your compliance team:

For 90 days, you operate under uncertainty. Tariff rates might change. Legal authority might shift. Your duty accrual assumptions are now in question.

That's not comfortable. But it's the reality.

Your 90-Day Action Plan

Week 1 (Now):

  1. Quantify IEEPA-related duties paid

  2. Gather refund documentation

  3. Decide refund strategy (direct request vs. protest vs. litigation)

  4. File if you're going the direct refund route (CBP will be flooded; get ahead of the queue)

Week 2-4:

  1. Monitor USTR announcements closely (they'll announce new tariff authority soon)

  2. Stress-test your tariff models against different scenarios (Section 301, Section 232, etc.)

  3. Update your landed cost calculations

  4. Brief procurement and finance on the tariff uncertainty window

Week 5-12:

  1. Adjust classification or sourcing assumptions as new authority becomes clear

  2. Revise tariff forecasts once new rates are announced

  3. Continue refund process (expect CBP to ask for additional documentation)

  4. Prepare your team for another round of tariff implementation once new authority is announced

The Broader Picture

This ruling is a wake-up call on tariff authority.

For 14 months, the administration used IEEPA to impose tariffs. It was fast. It was broad. It covered every sector. And it was legally shaky the whole time.

The court just confirmed it.

What does that mean for your compliance strategy going forward?

IEEPA tariffs are now off the table. Any future tariffs will have to go through narrower, more defensible legal authorities. That means they'll likely be more targeted (specific countries, specific products) rather than economy-wide.

Litigation risk is real. Whatever authority the administration uses next, expect challenges. Budget for legal risk. Assume some tariffs might not survive court review.

Tariff planning is now a multi-year process, not a one-time thing. You can't model tariffs for 2026-2028 based on today's rates. You have to model scenarios. Plan for uncertainty. Stay flexible.

Duty refunds are the closest thing to "free money" importers get. If you're eligible, claim them. Don't leave money on the table because you missed a deadline or didn't file the right paperwork.

What Your Team Should Do This Week

  1. Assign someone to own the refund process. File the claim. Track the response. You've got 90 days before CBP either approves or denies it.

  2. Update your tariff forecast. Remove IEEPA assumptions. Add scenarios for likely alternative authorities. Show procurement the range of possible duty costs.

  3. Brief your executive team. This isn't a compliance issue—it's a business issue. Tariff costs are now uncertain. Margin planning is now uncertain. Your CFO needs to know.

  4. Monitor USTR daily. The administration will announce new tariff authority within weeks. When they do, your team needs to understand the legal basis and what it covers.

This is a high-uncertainty window. But it's also an opportunity. Companies that move fast on refunds and prepare early for the next tariff regime will be better positioned than companies that wait.

Title: What AI Actually Means for Trade Compliance
SEO Title: AI in Trade Compliance: What It Means for Your Team
Story:
What AI Actually Means for Trade Compliance (And Why Most Companies Are Still Getting It Wrong)

Your compliance manager just spent 3 hours classifying a single product.

Not because they're slow. Because they had to search the HTSUS for applicable headings, read Section and Chapter Notes, dig through CROSS rulings for precedent, apply GRI 3(b) essential character analysis, and document the reasoning for audit defense.

Three hours. For one SKU.

Now multiply that by 500 new products this year. That's 1,500 hours. 37 work weeks. Almost an entire FTE just on classification.

And that's before tariff monitoring. Denied party screening. Duty drawback claims. FTA qualification. Audit prep.

This is why AI matters in trade compliance. Not because it's cool. Not because it's the future. Because right now, your compliance team is drowning in manual work that machines can do faster and more accurately.

But here's what most companies get wrong about AI in compliance. They think it's about replacement. It's not.

It's about giving your compliance professionals their time back so they can do the work that actually matters.

What AI Actually Is (Without the Hype)

Let's cut through the noise.

AI in trade compliance isn't magic. It's pattern recognition at scale. You train a model on hundreds of thousands of CBP rulings, tariff schedules, regulatory texts, and classification decisions. The model learns the patterns. Learns how GRI logic flows. Learns which material characteristics map to which HTS headings.

Then when you describe a product, the AI doesn't keyword search. It applies the same multi-step reasoning a trained analyst would use. But in 30 seconds instead of 90 minutes.

What makes it different from legacy automation:

Legacy platforms (SAP GTS, Descartes, Oracle GTM) automate workflows. They move data between systems. They enforce rules you manually configure. But they don't reason. They don't learn. They can't adapt when regulations change.

AI does. It references new rulings. Updates when tariff schedules shift. Explains its reasoning. Gets better with use.

That's the fundamental difference. Workflow automation moves boxes around. AI actually thinks through the problem.

Where AI Changes Trade Compliance Workflows

Let's talk specifics. Where does AI actually save time?

1. HTS Classification

Old workflow:

  1. Analyst reads product description

  2. Searches HTSUS for potential headings (30 min)

  3. Reads Section and Chapter Notes (20 min)

  4. Searches CROSS for similar products (30 min)

  5. Applies GRI logic to determine correct heading (20 min)

  6. Documents reasoning (10 min)

  7. Total: 110 minutes per product

AI workflow:

  1. Input product description

  2. AI asks clarifying questions based on GRI requirements

Title: The 25% AI Chip Tariff in 2026: What Businesses Need to Know

Story:
The 25% AI Chip Tariff: What You Need to Know for 2026

Introduction:

On January 14, 2026, the White House announced a major shift in the semiconductor trade landscape with the introduction of a 25% tariff on advanced AI chips under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act. This tariff affects high-performance chips like the Nvidia H200 and AMD MI325X, commonly used in data centers and artificial intelligence (AI) applications. If you're involved in the semiconductor industry or managing global supply chains, this tariff will impact how you approach imports, exports, and compliance.

In this post, we'll break down everything you need to know about this new tariff, who it affects, the potential exemptions, and how businesses can navigate this shifting trade policy.

What Is the 25% AI Chip Tariff and Why It Matters?

The 25% tariff on AI chips is part of an ongoing effort by the U.S. government to protect national security and strengthen domestic semiconductor production. This move comes as the U.S. faces growing competition from foreign manufacturers, especially in high-performance computing, which is critical for national security and technological leadership.

Key points of the tariff:

  • Effective from January 14, 2026, the tariff applies to certain advanced computing chips.

  • Affected chips include high-end accelerators like the Nvidia H200 and AMD MI325X, which are used in data centers and AI applications.

  • The tariff is set at 25% and will be automatically imposed upon arrival of these chips in the U.S. unless exemptions apply.

Who Is Affected by the 25% Tariff on AI Chips?

The new AI chip tariff is designed to target specific products, including high-performance chips used in AI accelerators and data centers. Here’s a breakdown of the industries and companies that will be directly impacted:

1. Semiconductor Manufacturers:

  • Companies like Nvidia and AMD that produce chips for AI and data center applications will see a significant cost increase when exporting these products to the U.S. These companies must adjust their strategies to account for the 25% tariff on their exports.

2. Importers and Exporters:

  • If you import AI chips into the U.S., be prepared for higher landed costs as a result of the tariff. This means you need to be clear on Incoterms to ensure everyone involved in the supply chain knows who bears the 25% tariff cost.

3. Compliance Professionals:

  • Those working in compliance and trade management will need to stay on top of Section 232 requirements, ensuring that products meet the proper certifications and exemptions to avoid tariffs where applicable.

4. U.S. Data Centers and Startups:

  • U.S.-based data centers and startups involved in research and development (R&D) may benefit from specific exemptions under the Proclamation.

Exemptions to the 25% AI Chip Tariff: Who Is Not Affected?

While the 25% tariff applies to advanced AI chips, there are important exemptions for certain types of imports. This includes chips that support the buildout of U.S. technology supply chains and domestic semiconductor manufacturing capacity. Here’s a closer look at the exemptions:

1. U.S. Technology Supply Chain Buildout:

  • Chips that are imported to support the U.S. technology supply chain and strengthen domestic semiconductor manufacturing are exempt from the 25% tariff. This means that components used to build semiconductor fabrication plants (fabs) or to support U.S. AI infrastructure are not subject to the tariff.

2. R&D Exemption:

  • U.S. startups, data centers, and companies involved in R&D can also qualify for exemptions. Chips used specifically for research or development (not production) are typically excluded from the tariff.

Note: Companies must document the purpose of their import to qualify for this exemption. Proper certifications and end-use statements will be required to avoid paying the tariff on R&D-related chips.

How Will the 25% Tariff Be Enforced?

The 25% tariff will be enforced through the Harmonized Tariff Schedule (HTS), which classifies products for import/export purposes. The key HTS classifications likely impacted include:

  • 8542.39.xx: Electronic integrated circuits (other)

  • 8542.31.xx / 8542.32.xx: Processors and controllers (whether or not combined with memory)

The Proclamation will clarify the exact HTS subheadings and performance thresholds that apply to AI chips. The tariff will apply to products that fall under these classifications unless they meet an exemption (such as being used in domestic semiconductor manufacturing or for R&D purposes).

What Should Businesses Do to Prepare?

As a business involved in the import/export or manufacturing of AI chips, there are several steps you can take to prepare for the impact of the new 25% tariff:

  1. Review Your Import/Export Contracts:

    • Make sure Incoterms are clear so that it’s obvious who is responsible for covering the tariff costs during the U.S. “pit stop.”

  2. Track HTS Codes and Classifications:

    • Stay updated on HTS codes and performance thresholds that will determine whether your products are subject to the tariff or eligible for exemptions.

  3. Consider Reworking Your Supply Chain:

    • If you’re heavily reliant on imports from foreign suppliers, you may need to adjust your supply chain to mitigate the impact of the tariff. For example, look for suppliers within the U.S. or in countries with favorable trade relations.

  4. Apply for Exemptions Where Applicable:

    • Ensure you are eligible for any exemptions (e.g., for R&D or domestic manufacturing) and gather the necessary documentation to apply for these exemptions.

The Impact of the 25% AI Chip Tariff: A Game Changer for the Semiconductor Industry

This new tariff will likely have a ripple effect on the global semiconductor industry, impacting AI chip production and supply chains. Companies that rely on importing high-performance AI chips may need to adjust their pricing strategies, supply chain logistics, and compliance processes.

As the U.S. government continues to prioritize domestic semiconductor manufacturing and technological sovereignty, we may see additional tariffs or regulatory changes in the future. Staying informed about these changes is critical for businesses that depend on these high-tech products.

Conclusion

The 25% AI chip tariff is a significant development that will reshape the landscape for chipmakers, importers, exporters, and companies involved in data center and AI infrastructure. While some may benefit from exemptions, others will face higher costs and more complex compliance procedures. Understanding the nuances of the tariff and preparing accordingly will help businesses navigate these changes effectively.

For more details, check out the official Proclamation here: White House Proclamation on Semiconductors.

Title: A Strategic Guide to Antidumping and Countervailing Duties (AD/CVD)
Story:
The Hidden Financial Liability in Global Trade: A Strategic Guide to Antidumping and Countervailing Duties (AD/CVD)

In the modern trade landscape, tariffs are often viewed as a fixed cost, usually a predictable percentage calculated at the time of entry. However, for strategic trade professionals, the true danger lies not in standard duties, but in the retrospective and punitive nature of Antidumping (AD) and Countervailing Duties (CVD).

Unlike Section 301 or Section 232 tariffs, AD/CVD rates are not static. They are estimated cash deposits subject to retroactive change, capable of generating liabilities that extend years into the future. For importers, mismanaging this area doesn’t just mean paying a higher rate; it means facing unbudgeted, six-figure bills long after the goods have been sold.

This guide explores the structural mechanics of AD/CVD, the specific "scope traps" that bypass standard classification controls, and the compliance strategies required to mitigate these high-stakes risks.

1. The Core Mechanic: Retrospective Liability

The fundamental misunderstanding of AD/CVD is that the duty paid at entry is final. It is not.

When an investigation reaches a Preliminary Determination, the Department of Commerce instructs Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to "suspend liquidation" and collect cash deposits. These deposits are merely estimates. The actual liability is determined during an Administrative Review, a process that occurs annually and can take over a year to finalize.

  • The Risk: If Commerce determines that dumping margins increased during the review period, importers are billed for the difference plus interest.

  • The Reality: An importer paying a 10% deposit today could receive a liquidation bill three years from now adjusting that rate to 150%.

  • Critical Circumstances: If importers attempt to surge shipments before a preliminary determination, Commerce can declare "Critical Circumstances." This allows CBP to apply duties retroactively to entries made 90 days prior to the suspension of liquidation.

2. The Scope Trap: Why HTS Codes Are Not Dispositive

In standard customs compliance, the Harmonized Tariff Schedule (HTS) code dictates the duty rate. In AD/CVD enforcement, the HTS code is largely irrelevant.

The Department of Commerce relies exclusively on the Written Scope of the order. This narrative description is legally "dispositive," meaning it overrides the tariff classification declared at entry.

Case Study: The "Hand Truck" Precedent

Consider the AD/CVD order on Hand Trucks from China (Case A-570-891). The scope explicitly covers hand trucks with a vertical frame and a "projecting edge or toe plate".

  • The Trap: An importer bringing in a "log carrier" or "luggage cart" may classify it under a generic metal furniture or cart HTS code that is not flagged for dumping.

  • The Liability: If the product physically matches the narrative description (two wheels, vertical frame, toe plate), it is subject to the order regardless of the HTS code used.

  • The Solution: Do not rely on broker software flags. You must analyze the physical characteristics of your product against the text of the petition.

3. The "Helpful Vendor" Trap: Reimbursement

Suppliers often attempt to mitigate the sting of high duties by offering to reimburse the importer. While this may seem commercially advantageous, it is strictly prohibited under U.S. law.

The purpose of AD/CVD is to increase the landing price of goods to fair market value. Reimbursement negates this remedy. Consequently, if an importer cannot prove they paid the duties themselves, CBP is authorized to double the dumping duties as a penalty.

Compliance Requirement: Importers must file a Non-Reimbursement Statement with the District Director of Customs annually. Failure to file this certificate results in a presumption of reimbursement and the automatic doubling of duties.

4. Strategic Mitigation: The Scope Ruling

When an importer’s product sits in the "grey area" of a written scope, uncertainty is a liability. The correct strategic move is often to file a Scope Ruling Request with the Department of Commerce.

A Scope Ruling is a binding determination that clarifies whether a specific product falls under an existing order.

  • Pro: It provides legal certainty and protection against future retroactive claims.

  • Con: It is a public process where domestic petitioners can argue against your exclusion.

5. Modern Solutions for Tariff Stacking

The complexity of managing standard duties alongside punitive AD/CVD rates creates a "tariff stacking" problem that breaks traditional spreadsheets. Calculating total landed cost now requires layering Section 301, Section 232, and variable AD/CVD rates simultaneously.

Recognizing this gap in the market, we are currently developing Tariff GingerControl, a dedicated engine designed to be the market’s most reliable tool for tariff stacking. While currently in early access, it is built to handle the multi-layered complexity that modern trade compliance demands.

  • Explore the tool here: https://tariff.gingercontrol.com/

Key Takeaways for Trade Leaders

  1. Audit Your Bond: AD/CVD liability can quickly saturate your customs bond. Surety companies may demand collateral (letters of credit) as rates rise.

  2. Monitor the Federal Register: Relying on broker notifications is insufficient. Active monitoring of case developments is required to foresee rate changes.

  3. Review Courier Entries: Express shipments (FedEx/DHL) often slip through compliance nets. Ensure these entries are audited for AD/CVD applicability.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q: Can I use Duty Drawback on Antidumping Duties?

A: No. Unlike standard Section 301 tariffs, AD/CVD duties are generally not eligible for duty drawback upon export, as they are considered remedial penalties rather than revenue-generating taxes.

Q: What is the statute of limitations on AD/CVD entries?

A: Because liquidation is suspended during the investigation and review periods, the standard 1-year liquidation cycle does not apply. Entries can remain open for years until the final litigation is resolved, keeping the statute of limitations effectively open indefinitely for those specific entries.

Q: How do I know if my product is subject to a case?

A: Do not rely solely on the HTS code. You must search the International Trade Administration (ITA) database or the ACE Portal (using the "References" tab) for cases related to your country of origin and commodity. Compare your product's physical specifications to the written scope of the order.

Title: How to Use CROSS for Tariff Classification
SEO Title: How to Use CROSS for HTS Tariff Classification
Story:
The Role of CROSS in HTS Classification

CROSS compiles decades of classification rulings into a searchable database. These rulings reveal how Customs interprets the Harmonized Tariff Schedule and applies the General Rules of Interpretation to actual products. They expose patterns in agency reasoning, show how physical characteristics are weighed, and demonstrate how comparable goods have been classified historically.

CROSS supports classification teams by:

  • Identifying the attributes that drove a classification decision, such as material makeup, essential character, or intended use

  • Resolving ambiguity in tariff language through documented precedent

  • Supplying citations to Notes and GRIs that explain the legal foundation of each ruling

  • Providing targeted comparisons for products that are complex or have multiple variants

CROSS does not override the GRIs or the statutory language of the HTS. It serves as an interpretive aid and a source of evidence when justifying internal decisions.

Searching CROSS Effectively

Basic keyword searches often fall short. Classification professionals get better results with a systematic approach.

A practical method includes:

  • Beginning with the product's fundamental characteristics: its function, what it's made of, how it's powered, and its physical form

  • Searching for rulings based on these attributes rather than brand names or marketing descriptions

  • Prioritizing recent rulings when agency interpretations have evolved or when the product involves emerging technology

  • Reading the entire ruling rather than just the conclusion, since the reasoning determines whether it applies to your situation

  • Recording all GRI and Note citations, as these explain the legal path Customs followed

Determining Whether a Ruling Applies to Your Product

A ruling is only relevant when its facts align with yours. Professionals should assess applicability using a consistent framework.

Consider the following:

  • Does the ruling address the same function and use scenario?

  • Are the materials and construction methods similar?

  • Does the ruling reference legal notes that apply to your product?

  • Does the essential character analysis follow logic that fits your goods?

  • Would any difference in technology, design, or configuration alter the outcome?

When a product differs materially from the ruling's facts, that precedent should not be treated as controlling.

Integrating CROSS with GRI Analysis

Rulings are valuable because they show GRI application in practice. Combining CROSS research with GRI reasoning produces a structured, defensible argument.

An effective workflow looks like this:

  • Start with GRI 1 and identify the tariff language that governs the product

  • Draw on CROSS rulings to support your interpretation of terms and descriptions

  • For composite or multifunctional goods, apply GRI 3 with examples from rulings that illustrate how Customs evaluated essential character

  • Confirm any analogies with citations to the legal text, rather than relying on precedent alone

Using CROSS to Strengthen Product Data

Many classification errors stem from incomplete or unclear product information. CROSS serves as a useful reference because it shows how Customs expects products to be described.

Rulings typically emphasize:

  • Specific, measurable characteristics

  • Materials that influence classification outcomes

  • Functional differences that distinguish one tariff line from another

  • Configurations or variants that change the legal analysis

Creating Audit-Ready Documentation with CROSS

Compliance programs depend on memos that explain why a particular code was chosen. CROSS adds credibility to these memos when incorporated correctly.

A strong classification memo should contain:

  • A detailed product description supported by internal data

  • The GRI logic applied in sequence

  • Relevant CROSS rulings with citations to the key reasoning

  • An explanation of how the ruling's facts compare to your product

  • Version control indicating when the analysis was completed and any subsequent updates

When CROSS Should Not Drive the Classification

Rulings have limitations. They may be outdated, narrowly fact-specific, or superseded by subsequent legal changes. Teams should avoid:

  • Relying on rulings that contradict the statutory text

  • Treating rulings as automatic answers without comparing the facts

  • Applying old rulings to modern products without considering technological changes

  • Using CROSS as a replacement for GRI analysis

CROSS is a supporting resource, not the legal authority itself.

Final Thoughts

CROSS is a valuable tool for building consistent, defensible HTS classifications. When combined with disciplined GRI analysis, thorough product data, and clear documentation, rulings help teams minimize risk, align decision-making across the organization, and establish audit-ready compliance processes that scale. Title: The $1,700 Hidden Tax Every US Family Pays
